papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation in Modern Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a foundational technique for compressing large neural models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision and language tasks, distillation can act both as a compression mechanism and as a regularizer, and it integrates naturally with complementary strategies such as architecture search, layer-wise alignment, representation matching, data augmentation, pruning, and deployment-aware methods. When applied thoughtfully—matching teacher and student representations, tuning the signal provided by soft labels, and adapting to task or device constraints—distillation enables practical, high-performing compressed models suitable for production and edge settings.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Practical Case for Knowledge Distillation in NLP: Effectiveness, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are a practical and necessary pathway to deploy high-performing pre-trained language models in resource-constrained settings. Distillation enables large teacher models to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations to smaller students, preserving much of the original performance while reducing inference cost. However, the success of distillation depends on choices across pre-training, teacher strength, layer- and feature-level alignment, data used for transfer, and augmentation or curriculum strategies. When these components are designed together, distilled models can approach teacher-level performance and enable real-world NLP systems at lower latency and cost.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Effective Knowledge Distillation for Deployable Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool to compress large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, KD has enabled domain adaptation, model-size reduction, cross-lingual transfer, and deployment under resource constraints. Success depends on (1) aligning teacher and student inputs and intermediate representations, (2) choosing appropriate supervision signals (soft labels, intermediate-feature losses, attention-based guidance), (3) handling the absence of original training data when necessary, and (4) adapting compression to task and domain requirements. This review synthesizes empirical and methodological findings from recent studies to recommend principled KD choices for practitioners aiming to deploy compact, robust models in real-world NLP and related tasks.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer information from larger, more expensive models to smaller, cheaper models to reduce inference cost while retaining accuracy. Across computer vision, speech, recommender systems and natural language processing, KD variants have targeted soft-label transfer, relational or feature imitation, self-distillation, and teacher adaptation to improve student generalization. Practical work emphasizes complementary strategies — pretraining compact architectures, specialist teacher training, careful input augmentation, and training-time efficiency — to address optimization mismatch, domain shift, and computational overhead. Remaining challenges include imperfect matching between teacher and student distributions, choosing data and augmentation strategies that preserve useful teacher signals, and designing distillation procedures that scale to constrained hardware and domain-specific needs.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Insights in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer useful information from larger, more expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable models. Research spans theoretical analyses of what is transferred, architectural and loss-design strategies to improve feature and output matching, specialized teacher–student training regimes (including multi-teacher and student-aware teacher training), online and federated distillation for large-scale or privacy-sensitive settings, and structural compression strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing memory and compute. Applications include image models, generative models, question-answering systems and multi-task natural language understanding, with methods tailored to domain constraints such as heterogeneous device capabilities and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compress large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD techniques that move beyond naive logit matching — for example by mimicking intermediate features, adapting teacher-student interactions to the task, or training teachers that are optimized for transfer — yield larger gains in both vision and language settings. KD also enables new training regimes (online and distributed) and can be combined with architecture search to produce task-aware compressed models. At the same time, interactions between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing) and the choice of what and how to transfer require careful design. Overall, KD is a mature and expanding toolkit that, when applied with methodical choices about knowledge type, teacher strategy, and training setup, provides an effective path to deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: The Pragmatic Power and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a practical toolkit for shrinking models, transferring behavior across architectures and modalities, and enabling deployment under compute, memory, or privacy constraints. Beyond straightforward teacher-to-student compression, distillation techniques combine with data augmentation, synthetic-data generation, and regularization to address limited data, cross-domain gaps, and interpretability needs. However, outcomes depend on choices about teacher quality, training data availability, and objective design; careful method selection is required to realize reliable, production-ready gains.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation can be combined with architectural replacement, layer mapping, and task-adaptive search to produce compact models that meet latency and capacity constraints. However, the benefits of distillation depend strongly on teacher quality, data complexity, and which examples or representations are used for transfer; naive application can propagate teacher errors or harm low-frequency predictions. Careful design—using task-aware compression, selective or mixed supervision, and targeted remedies for dataset artifacts—enables distillation to deliver efficient, robust models for real-world NLP and vision systems.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expressive models to smaller, efficient models to enable practical deployment without excessive loss in performance. These methods include matching teacher soft outputs, feature-level alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and architecture-aware strategies for heterogeneous settings. Across domains—vision, speech, NLP, and recommender systems—distillation is used both to compress models for latency and memory constraints and to inject complementary knowledge (e.g., cross-task or cross-modal signals). Empirical work shows that careful design choices (e.g., mixing hard/soft targets, projector modules, or student-aware teacher training) and task-specific adaptations address common pitfalls such as information loss on rare tokens or domain shifts. Open directions include stronger theoretical understanding, robustness under imperfect teachers, and principled integration with quantization, federated settings, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Current Understandings of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used model compression paradigm in which a smaller student model is trained to capture the behavior of a larger teacher model. It has been applied across domains (vision, NLP, recommender systems, medical imaging) to reduce model size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Work in the field explores what is transferred (soft outputs, internal representations, feature relations), how to improve transfer (adversarial samples, contrastive objectives, structural transformations), and how to address practical constraints (absence of original data, domain shift, privacy, fairness and robustness). Empirical results show KD often yields substantial memory and runtime benefits with modest accuracy loss and can be combined with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Yet KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, imperfect teacher signals, and mismatches between teacher and student capacity can limit how closely a student matches a teacher; research continues into theoretical explanations and robust, data-efficient methods.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile technique for shrinking large neural models while preserving much of their predictive power. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a pragmatic and flexible approach to compressing large neural models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in size and compute while retaining much of a teacher model's performance, and it adapts well to modalities from vision to speech and to task-specific constraints in NLP. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, mismatches between teacher and student, and the potential for poorer outcomes when distilling inappropriate teacher signals require careful method selection and evaluation. Best practice therefore combines tailored distillation architectures, curriculum or multi-teacher strategies, privacy-aware mechanisms where needed, and awareness of when label-smoothing or teacher-free alternatives are preferable.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a single-teacher trick into a versatile family of methods that enable deployable, compact models across vision and language tasks. Empirical work across domains shows that distillation benefits from adopting strategies that reflect (1) where the student starts (pre-training), (2) what signals it receives (single, multi- or ensemble teachers; feature- and layer-level targets), and (3) the constraints of the deployment context (limited or no access to real data, heterogenous devices, or federated settings). Combining these insights yields practical recipes that reliably close the gap between large models and resource-constrained students while preserving robustness and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques seek to reduce the runtime, memory, and deployment costs of large deep models while retaining their predictive performance or improving other desiderata (e.g., interpretability, fairness). Across vision and language domains, methods range from classical teacher-to-student soft-target distillation to transferring intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, selective sample-driven distillation, and teacher-adaptive or teacher-free schemes. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, alignment of intermediate representations, and input-side practices (such as tailored data augmentation) can materially affect student performance. Remaining challenges include representation mismatches between teacher and student, identifying which training samples are beneficial for transfer, and adapting distillation to domain- or resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or multi-modal models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural insights. Research has developed diverse KD variants—soft-label distillation, internal and layer-wise imitation, task-aware filtering, data-free distillation, and architecture-search guided compression—each addressing optimization, data availability, or deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs between matching teacher outputs and student generalization, the value of pre-training compact models, and the importance of choosing what and how knowledge is transferred to maximize downstream task performance while meeting resource limits.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile technique for shrinking large neural models while preserving much of their predictive power. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical paradigm for compressing and accelerating large deep models by transferring information from a cumbersome teacher to a compact student. Across modalities and tasks—supervised classification, representation learning, structured prediction, and generation—research shows KD can produce lightweight models that approach teacher performance, recover performance of small architectures, or enable new deployment constraints (privacy, federated settings). However, success depends critically on what is distilled (outputs, intermediate representations, attention across layers), the data or metadata available for distillation, and the learning dynamics between teacher and student. Open challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, and designing teachers or distillation procedures that reliably transfer the right kind of knowledge for a target student capacity and deployment setting.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying deep models under resource constraints. Methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-layer supervision, feature mimicking, projector-based transforms, teacher-student co-training, and data- or domain-aware schemes. Distillation has been applied across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs) and in settings with limited or no access to original training data. Practical advances address transfer across architectures, task-adaptive compression, and efficient architecture search, while open problems remain around distribution shift, heterogeneity of data or detectors, and preserving rare or low-frequency information.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, insights, and practical trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in latency-, memory-, and compute-constrained settings. Work across speech, NLP, vision, and graph domains demonstrates a spectrum of approaches: matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate features, progressively replacing modules, augmenting or synthesizing training data for better student generalization, and compressing ensembles into single models. Empirical results show substantial speed and size gains with modest accuracy loss when methods are carefully matched to task and architecture. Important themes include (1) the role of dark/soft labels vs. intermediate feature signals, (2) architectural or task-aware compression (including search), (3) techniques that increase the student’s exposure to informative training points (e.g., mixup or adversarial examples), and (4) distillation strategies tailored for ensembles or heterogeneous teacher–student pairs. Open challenges remain in principled sample selection, robust transfer of inductive biases, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing modern deep models across modalities. When combined with architecture-aware transformations, feature-level supervision, multi-teacher signals, and careful handling of data constraints, KD enables compact students that retain most of a teacher's effectiveness while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, distillation artifacts and data limitations require methodic choices—e.g., feature mimicking, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, or generative replay—to avoid propagating teacher errors or overfitting in low-data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression are indispensable tools to deploy high-performing deep models under compute, memory, privacy, and latency constraints. Across modalities and tasks, effective compression requires more than copying teacher logits: practitioners should match richer internal representations, align inputs and tokenization across teacher and student, design teacher updates that explicitly optimize transfer, and account for privacy and robustness needs. When applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that retain much of the teacher’s utility and in some cases improve efficiency beyond the original models.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Methods and Challenges in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across vision, generative modeling, and NLP, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, task-specific adaptations, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher-optimization strategies to improve student accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Work also focuses on constraints arising in distributed and privacy-preserving settings, on preserving rare or fine-grained information, and on adapting distillation to complex tasks such as detection, generation, and dense prediction. Practical systems combine architectural choices, training curricula, and distilled supervision to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: Practical, Theoretical, and Methodological Evidence for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and mature approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from richer teacher models to compact students. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, vision, graph learning, and retrieval—KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher's performance. Beyond pure compression, KD variants address practical deployment concerns: multi-teacher and confidence-aware schemes improve robustness to imperfect teachers; progressive and module-level replacement approaches enable deeper integrated compression; online/distillation-in-parallel techniques scale training and improve reproducibility; and targeted feature-distillation methods refine representational quality. Theory of wide networks provides guidance on when soft labels help and when mixing hard labels is beneficial. Together, empirical and theoretical work shows KD is a versatile, well-grounded toolbox for model compression and knowledge transfer in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Compression, Regularization, and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression heuristic into a versatile training paradigm that enables model size reduction, improved generalization, domain adaptation, and task consolidation. Its practical success depends on both the sources of teacher supervision (final logits, intermediate representations, or multiple teachers) and how distillation is applied (sample selection, layer matching, or label design). While KD frequently yields compact, high-performing models, its benefits arise from a mixture of transferred dark knowledge and regularizing effects of soft targets; careful design choices are required to realize those benefits across settings such as language model compression, multi-task training, and privacy-constrained or heterogeneous environments.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller ones by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from a teacher to a student. Over the past decade KD methods have diversified beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher pipelines, data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical work across NLP, speech, vision-language, and other domains shows KD can preserve most of a teacher's performance while drastically reducing model size and latency. Theoretical and empirical analyses have clarified why KD works in many settings (regularization via soft targets, ensemble-induced dark knowledge, and representation enrichment), but open problems remain in data privacy, distribution shift, automated student design, and guarantees for out-of-distribution robustness.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, cheaper models (students) by using richer supervision than hard labels alone. The literature has developed multiple complementary strategies—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, architecturally guided replacement, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and teacher-training schemes—to address deployment constraints, domain shift, and limited or private data. Empirical work shows these approaches can close much of the performance gap to full-size models across classification, language understanding, and retrieval tasks; theoretical and empirical analyses explain why distillation often improves generalization beyond mere compression. Remaining challenges include input distribution mismatch, low-frequency token fidelity in sequence tasks, and robust distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compact, Robust, and Adaptable Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers while enabling domain adaptation, deployment under resource constraints, privacy-preserving releases, and improved robustness. KD techniques span transfer from full teacher ensembles to single students, intermediate-layer alignment, self-distillation, and even data-free distillation; each variant addresses different operational constraints. However, distillation also carries risks (e.g., transfer of undesirable biases) and requires careful design choices (e.g., what information to transfer and what data to use). Combining advances across these variants yields effective, small NLP models fit for real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while preserving performance, enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, and domain-specific constraints. Across modalities and tasks, KD can be combined with architectural search, feature-level objectives, teacher optimization, and data-free methods to meet diverse production requirements. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a primary instrument in model-compression toolkits for modern deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic training trick into a unifying framework for producing compact, efficient models across vision, speech, and language tasks. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus from larger teachers to smaller students, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving accuracy. Beyond plain size reduction, KD adapts to constraints that arise in real deployments — limited data or privacy-sensitive settings, heterogeneous architectures, and modality gaps — through techniques such as feature-level alignment, selective sampling, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data-free synthesis. As a practical bridge between research-scale architectures and deployable systems, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and serves both as an efficiency accelerator and as a lever for robustness and domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

                    [{'author': 'Miller', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering', 'abstract': 'Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents.
