Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and easier deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings. When combined with teacher ensembles, online or self-distillation, task-adaptive search, and careful handling of soft labels and data augmentation, distillation can deliver near-teacher accuracy while addressing scalability, robustness, and domain transfer concerns. I argue that knowledge distillation should be a first-line approach for model compression in modern NLP pipelines, supplemented by principled choices about teachers, data, and optimization to realize its full benefits.'}, {'author': 'Davidson', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical paradigm for compressing and accelerating large deep models by transferring information from a cumbersome teacher to a compact student. Across modalities and tasks—supervised classification, representation learning, structured prediction, and generation—research shows KD can produce lightweight models that approach teacher performance, recover performance of small architectures, or enable new deployment constraints (privacy, federated settings). However, success depends critically on what is distilled (outputs, intermediate representations, attention across layers), the data or metadata available for distillation, and the learning dynamics between teacher and student. Open challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, and designing teachers or distillation procedures that reliably transfer the right kind of knowledge for a target student capacity and deployment setting.'}, {'author': 'Henderson', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying deep models under resource constraints. Methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-layer supervision, feature mimicking, projector-based transforms, teacher-student co-training, and data- or domain-aware schemes. Distillation has been applied across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs) and in settings with limited or no access to original training data. Practical advances address transfer across architectures, task-adaptive compression, and efficient architecture search, while open problems remain around distribution shift, heterogeneity of data or detectors, and preserving rare or low-frequency information.'}, {'author': 'Rios', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.'}, {'author': 'Gardner', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Adversarially Robust Distillation', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.'}, {'author': 'Cannon', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, insights, and practical trends', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in latency-, memory-, and compute-constrained settings. Work across speech, NLP, vision, and graph domains demonstrates a spectrum of approaches: matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate features, progressively replacing modules, augmenting or synthesizing training data for better student generalization, and compressing ensembles into single models. Empirical results show substantial speed and size gains with modest accuracy loss when methods are carefully matched to task and architecture. Important themes include (1) the role of dark/soft labels vs. intermediate feature signals, (2) architectural or task-aware compression (including search), (3) techniques that increase the student’s exposure to informative training points (e.g., mixup or adversarial examples), and (4) distillation strategies tailored for ensembles or heterogeneous teacher–student pairs. Open challenges remain in principled sample selection, robust transfer of inductive biases, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.'}, {'author': 'Fowler', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing modern deep models across modalities. When combined with architecture-aware transformations, feature-level supervision, multi-teacher signals, and careful handling of data constraints, KD enables compact students that retain most of a teacher's effectiveness while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, distillation artifacts and data limitations require methodic choices—e.g., feature mimicking, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, or generative replay—to avoid propagating teacher errors or overfitting in low-data regimes."}, {'author': 'Smith', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression are indispensable tools to deploy high-performing deep models under compute, memory, privacy, and latency constraints. Across modalities and tasks, effective compression requires more than copying teacher logits: practitioners should match richer internal representations, align inputs and tokenization across teacher and student, design teacher updates that explicitly optimize transfer, and account for privacy and robustness needs. When applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that retain much of the teacher’s utility and in some cases improve efficiency beyond the original models.'}, {'author': 'James', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation', 'abstract': 'The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.'}, {'author': 'Williams', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Contemporary Methods and Challenges in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across vision, generative modeling, and NLP, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, task-specific adaptations, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher-optimization strategies to improve student accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Work also focuses on constraints arising in distributed and privacy-preserving settings, on preserving rare or fine-grained information, and on adapting distillation to complex tasks such as detection, generation, and dense prediction. Practical systems combine architectural choices, training curricula, and distilled supervision to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for deployment.'}, {'author': 'Arnold', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'The Case for Knowledge Distillation: Practical, Theoretical, and Methodological Evidence for Efficient Deep Models', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and mature approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from richer teacher models to compact students. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, vision, graph learning, and retrieval—KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher's performance. Beyond pure compression, KD variants address practical deployment concerns: multi-teacher and confidence-aware schemes improve robustness to imperfect teachers; progressive and module-level replacement approaches enable deeper integrated compression; online/distillation-in-parallel techniques scale training and improve reproducibility; and targeted feature-distillation methods refine representational quality. Theory of wide networks provides guidance on when soft labels help and when mixing hard labels is beneficial. Together, empirical and theoretical work shows KD is a versatile, well-grounded toolbox for model compression and knowledge transfer in modern deep learning."}, {'author': 'Bowman', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations', 'abstract': 'Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.'}, {'author': 'Perez', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors', 'abstract': 'To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \\url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.'}, {'author': 'Davis', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': "Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one."}, {'author': 'Parsons', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation', 'abstract': "Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework."}, {'author': 'Martin', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.'}, {'author': 'Cohen', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques."}, {'author': 'Hahn', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\\% and 4.8\\% higher than the baseline, respectively.'}, {'author': 'Shaffer', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.'}, {'author': 'Graham', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Compression, Regularization, and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression heuristic into a versatile training paradigm that enables model size reduction, improved generalization, domain adaptation, and task consolidation. Its practical success depends on both the sources of teacher supervision (final logits, intermediate representations, or multiple teachers) and how distillation is applied (sample selection, layer matching, or label design). While KD frequently yields compact, high-performing models, its benefits arise from a mixture of transferred dark knowledge and regularizing effects of soft targets; careful design choices are required to realize those benefits across settings such as language model compression, multi-task training, and privacy-constrained or heterogeneous environments.'}, {'author': 'Rice', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practice', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller ones by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from a teacher to a student. Over the past decade KD methods have diversified beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-feature imitation, multi-teacher pipelines, data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical work across NLP, speech, vision-language, and other domains shows KD can preserve most of a teacher's performance while drastically reducing model size and latency. Theoretical and empirical analyses have clarified why KD works in many settings (regularization via soft targets, ensemble-induced dark knowledge, and representation enrichment), but open problems remain in data privacy, distribution shift, automated student design, and guarantees for out-of-distribution robustness."}, {'author': 'Wright', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, cheaper models (students) by using richer supervision than hard labels alone. The literature has developed multiple complementary strategies—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, architecturally guided replacement, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and teacher-training schemes—to address deployment constraints, domain shift, and limited or private data. Empirical work shows these approaches can close much of the performance gap to full-size models across classification, language understanding, and retrieval tasks; theoretical and empirical analyses explain why distillation often improves generalization beyond mere compression. Remaining challenges include input distribution mismatch, low-frequency token fidelity in sequence tasks, and robust distillation without access to original training data.'}, {'author': 'Tucker', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compact, Robust, and Adaptable Deep Models in NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers while enabling domain adaptation, deployment under resource constraints, privacy-preserving releases, and improved robustness. KD techniques span transfer from full teacher ensembles to single students, intermediate-layer alignment, self-distillation, and even data-free distillation; each variant addresses different operational constraints. However, distillation also carries risks (e.g., transfer of undesirable biases) and requires careful design choices (e.g., what information to transfer and what data to use). Combining advances across these variants yields effective, small NLP models fit for real-world constraints.'}, {'author': 'Davis', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while preserving performance, enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, and domain-specific constraints. Across modalities and tasks, KD can be combined with architectural search, feature-level objectives, teacher optimization, and data-free methods to meet diverse production requirements. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a primary instrument in model-compression toolkits for modern deep learning and NLP systems.'}, {'author': 'Martin', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR', 'abstract': 'Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.'}, {'author': 'Dudley', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as the Core Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic training trick into a unifying framework for producing compact, efficient models across vision, speech, and language tasks. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus from larger teachers to smaller students, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving accuracy. Beyond plain size reduction, KD adapts to constraints that arise in real deployments — limited data or privacy-sensitive settings, heterogeneous architectures, and modality gaps — through techniques such as feature-level alignment, selective sampling, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data-free synthesis. As a practical bridge between research-scale architectures and deployable systems, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and serves both as an efficiency accelerator and as a lever for robustness and domain generalization.'}, {'author': 'Valencia', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.'}, {'author': 'Herrera', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN\'s compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.'}, {'author': 'Brown', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Unified Visual Transformer Compression', 'abstract': 'Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.'}]

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD techniques span soft-label transfer, intermediate representation matching, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, and adaptations for constrained or distributed settings. When combined with careful pretraining, representation-aware losses, selective sample strategies, and attention to privacy or robustness requirements, KD enables practical deployment of high-quality models on resource-limited devices and in federated environments.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teacher's performance. When combined with complementary strategies — such as careful layer mapping, pre-training of compact models, multi-teacher schedules, privacy-aware mechanisms, and synthetic-data techniques — distillation addresses the principal deployment barriers of modern deep networks: inference cost, data access constraints, and heterogeneous compute environments. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit that can be adapted to the needs of NLP and general deep learning applications to produce compact, robust, and privacy-conscious models.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, cheaper models (students) by using richer supervision than hard labels alone. The literature has developed multiple complementary strategies—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, architecturally guided replacement, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and teacher-training schemes—to address deployment constraints, domain shift, and limited or private data. Empirical work shows these approaches can close much of the performance gap to full-size models across classification, language understanding, and retrieval tasks; theoretical and empirical analyses explain why distillation often improves generalization beyond mere compression. Remaining challenges include input distribution mismatch, low-frequency token fidelity in sequence tasks, and robust distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD has been applied successfully to compress large language models, vision transformers, and task-specific architectures, and adapted to settings including self-supervision, multi-task learning, and privacy-sensitive or data-limited regimes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on the alignment between teacher and student architectures, the availability and quality of data (or of synthetic surrogates), the selection of what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), and task-specific choices such as layer-wise matching and curriculum. Recognizing both the demonstrated strengths and the practical failure modes of KD leads to targeted best practices: choose distillation targets that match the student capacity and task, use task-aware or feature-focused objectives for intermediate representations, apply adversarial or synthetic data approaches when original data are unavailable, and explicitly evaluate KD under realistic heterogeneity (e.g., federated or multi-task) to avoid hidden degradations.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, insights, and practical trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in latency-, memory-, and compute-constrained settings. Work across speech, NLP, vision, and graph domains demonstrates a spectrum of approaches: matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate features, progressively replacing modules, augmenting or synthesizing training data for better student generalization, and compressing ensembles into single models. Empirical results show substantial speed and size gains with modest accuracy loss when methods are carefully matched to task and architecture. Important themes include (1) the role of dark/soft labels vs. intermediate feature signals, (2) architectural or task-aware compression (including search), (3) techniques that increase the student’s exposure to informative training points (e.g., mixup or adversarial examples), and (4) distillation strategies tailored for ensembles or heterogeneous teacher–student pairs. Open challenges remain in principled sample selection, robust transfer of inductive biases, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central to deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, practical algorithms for distilling logits, representations, and attention, techniques that require no original data, and adaptations for domains such as NLP, machine translation, and distributed training. Empirical work has shown KD can both accelerate inference and enable smaller models to approach or even exceed teacher performance in some settings, while recent advances address domain adaptivity, robustness, and teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a unifying, practical framework to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while addressing concerns of computation, privacy, robustness, and limited task data. KD techniques span from logits- and feature-based matching to progressive module replacement, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free (zero-shot) synthesis, and federated output-sharing, and when combined with careful data augmentation and generative replay they yield compact models that retain much of the teacher utility in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques seek to reduce the runtime, memory, and deployment costs of large deep models while retaining their predictive performance or improving other desiderata (e.g., interpretability, fairness). Across vision and language domains, methods range from classical teacher-to-student soft-target distillation to transferring intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, selective sample-driven distillation, and teacher-adaptive or teacher-free schemes. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, alignment of intermediate representations, and input-side practices (such as tailored data augmentation) can materially affect student performance. Remaining challenges include representation mismatches between teacher and student, identifying which training samples are beneficial for transfer, and adapting distillation to domain- or resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a pragmatic and flexible approach to compressing large neural models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in size and compute while retaining much of a teacher model's performance, and it adapts well to modalities from vision to speech and to task-specific constraints in NLP. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, mismatches between teacher and student, and the potential for poorer outcomes when distilling inappropriate teacher signals require careful method selection and evaluation. Best practice therefore combines tailored distillation architectures, curriculum or multi-teacher strategies, privacy-aware mechanisms where needed, and awareness of when label-smoothing or teacher-free alternatives are preferable.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. KD is applicable across modalities and tasks, from machine translation and reading comprehension to distributed training and privacy-sensitive deployment. Success depends on aligning teacher and student representations, selecting appropriate knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention, contrastive signals), and matching methods to constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy requirements. Theoretical analyses and practical advances both show that careful design choices — including attention-based matching, layer projection, task-aware filtering, online collaboration, multi-teacher weighting, and privacy-aware perturbation — materially affect outcomes and trade-offs between fidelity, efficiency, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical paradigm for compressing and accelerating large deep models by transferring information from a cumbersome teacher to a compact student. Across modalities and tasks—supervised classification, representation learning, structured prediction, and generation—research shows KD can produce lightweight models that approach teacher performance, recover performance of small architectures, or enable new deployment constraints (privacy, federated settings). However, success depends critically on what is distilled (outputs, intermediate representations, attention across layers), the data or metadata available for distillation, and the learning dynamics between teacher and student. Open challenges include optimization barriers that prevent exact teacher matching, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, and designing teachers or distillation procedures that reliably transfer the right kind of knowledge for a target student capacity and deployment setting.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, deployable models. Across computer vision, speech, recommendation, and natural language tasks, KD has been used to reduce inference cost while retaining most of the teacher model's performance. Research has advanced along several complementary axes: (1) methods that shape what is transferred (logits, hidden representations, attention or task-specific signals), (2) how the transfer is performed (layer-wise, multi-teacher, adversarial or student-aware training), (3) strategies to cope with limited or no access to original training data, and (4) techniques that preserve privacy and improve training efficiency. These lines of work show that careful alignment of objectives, attention to capacity gaps between teacher and student, and tailoring distillation to task and data regimes are critical for effective compression. Remaining challenges include robust cross-domain transfer, principled selection of what to distill for a target task, and maintaining robustness and fairness in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transform large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster, and more deployable models while attempting to preserve accuracy and useful inductive biases. Approaches span classic teacher–student logit matching, representation and feature imitation, layer mapping strategies for large pretrained language models, data-free and zero-shot methods that avoid access to original training data, and privacy- or communication-aware frameworks for distributed settings. Empirical work demonstrates these methods can yield practical speedups, substantial parameter reductions, and competitive task performance across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks; theoretical and empirical studies also clarify when softened teacher targets or distilled datasets best help student capacity. Remaining challenges include balancing privacy and utility, reducing the cost of distillation when teachers are large, and extending guarantees and methods across modalities and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Compressing Visual-linguistic Model via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite exciting progress in pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations, very few aspire to a small VL model. In this paper, we study knowledge distillation (KD) to effectively compress a transformer-based large VL model into a small VL model. The major challenge arises from the inconsistent regional visual tokens extracted from different detectors of Teacher and Student, resulting in the misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions. To address the problem, we retrain and adapt the Teacher by using the same region proposals from Student's detector while the features are from Teacher's own object detector. With aligned network inputs, the adapted Teacher is capable of transferring the knowledge through the intermediate representations. Specifically, we use the mean square error loss to mimic the attention distribution inside the transformer block and present a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align the hidden state by contrasting with negative representations stored in a sample queue. To this end, we show that our proposed distillation significantly improves the performance of small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks. It reaches 120.8 in CIDEr score on COCO captioning, an improvement of 5.1 over its non-distilled counterpart; and an accuracy of 69.8 on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 gain from the baseline. Our extensive experiments and ablations confirm the effectiveness of VL distillation in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Practical Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster models suitable for production and edge deployment. Different KD variants—data-free, multi-teacher, online, feature-level, adversarial, and task-specific strategies—address practical constraints like lack of original data, communication or privacy limits, and the need to preserve representational quality. However, KD is not a panacea: its benefits depend on teacher-student capacity, dataset complexity, optimization choices, and the design of distillation signals. A pragmatic approach selects KD variants that match the application constraints and explicitly addresses optimization and data-complexity issues to maximize student performance while preserving efficiency and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and broadly applicable technique to compress large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Work across computer vision, speech, and natural language processing demonstrates that KD can enable deployment of resource-efficient models, improve generalization in constrained settings, and be combined with other compression methods (e.g., low-precision numerics). At the same time, the field has identified important limitations and nuanced behaviors — such as data simplification effects, teacher–student mismatches, and domain or task-specific failure modes — that guide how KD should be applied in practice. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, variants, empirical benefits, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.
