papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques enable deployment of large neural models by transferring knowledge from larger or multi-modal teachers to smaller or specialized students. Work in this area spans methods for structural student design, feature- and logit-level supervision, data-free or few-shot settings, low-precision inference, multi-teacher and domain-adaptive strategies, and automated discovery of compact architectures. Empirical results across vision, speech, language, graph, and generative models show that distillation often achieves substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while preserving much of the teacher performance; however, success depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, and training protocols. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, efficient training when teacher cost is high, and principled methods for combining multiple or heterogeneous teachers.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Compression, Regularization, and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression heuristic into a versatile training paradigm that enables model size reduction, improved generalization, domain adaptation, and task consolidation. Its practical success depends on both the sources of teacher supervision (final logits, intermediate representations, or multiple teachers) and how distillation is applied (sample selection, layer matching, or label design). While KD frequently yields compact, high-performing models, its benefits arise from a mixture of transferred dark knowledge and regularizing effects of soft targets; careful design choices are required to realize those benefits across settings such as language model compression, multi-task training, and privacy-constrained or heterogeneous environments.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a single compression trick but a flexible set of techniques that can reduce model size, preserve or transfer task-relevant information, enable deployment in latency- and memory-constrained settings, support domain adaptation and privacy-preserving federated workflows, and be combined with structural compression. When applied thoughtfully — with task-aware selection of distilled signals, architecturally informed teacher-student design, and attention to data availability and optimization dynamics — KD yields large practical benefits for deep learning and NLP systems while avoiding common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models for deployment, while preserving performance and enabling new capabilities such as efficient federated learning, data-free compression, interpretability, and few-shot adaptation. Across architectures and tasks, KD variants—ranging from layer-to-layer alignment and progressive module replacement to meta-learned teachers and adversarial data synthesis—provide methods to trade computation, memory, and communication for small changes in accuracy. These methods make it possible to bring large pretrained models into production and edge settings, and to reconcile competing requirements such as privacy, heterogeneity, and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a pragmatic and flexible approach to compressing large neural models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in size and compute while retaining much of a teacher model's performance, and it adapts well to modalities from vision to speech and to task-specific constraints in NLP. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, mismatches between teacher and student, and the potential for poorer outcomes when distilling inappropriate teacher signals require careful method selection and evaluation. Best practice therefore combines tailored distillation architectures, curriculum or multi-teacher strategies, privacy-aware mechanisms where needed, and awareness of when label-smoothing or teacher-free alternatives are preferable.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable smaller or faster models to retain much of the performance of larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or task-specific inductive biases. Work in this area spans supervised soft-target matching, intermediate-layer representation transfer, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble-derived strategies, and online/distributed variants that exploit parallelism. Applications include compressing large pretrained language models for downstream NLP tasks, accelerating inference for computer vision and generative models, and producing interpretable or privacy-preserving compact models for healthcare and on-device deployment. Important trade-offs involve what form of knowledge is transferred (logits, activations, relations), access to training data, robustness to domain heterogeneity, and how to balance capacity, efficiency, and generalization in student models.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Work across vision and language shows a set of recurring strategies: transfer using softened outputs (soft targets), imitation of intermediate/internal representations, layer mapping between teacher and student, task-adaptive architecture search, self-distillation, and data-free distillation when original training data are unavailable. Empirical results indicate that properly designed distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while offering large gains in inference speed and memory; however, success depends on which knowledge is transferred (outputs vs. internal features), how layers are aligned, and whether task specificity and data availability are addressed. The field currently balances practical engineering (architecture and search) with algorithmic refinements (losses and training regimes), and open challenges include robust data-free methods, principled many-to-many layer matching, and teacher designs that are optimized to be “student-friendly.”

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher-student training recipe into a multifaceted toolkit that enables efficient, robust, and privacy-aware deployment of deep models. KD not only compresses large models into faster, smaller students suitable for edge and production, but also enables task-adaptive compression, data-limited or data-free scenarios, privacy-preserving federated setups, and transfers of inductive biases across architectures. When combined with complementary techniques such as architecture search, specialized feature-matching losses, and careful input-side interventions, KD yields practical compressed models without prohibitive losses in accuracy and can improve generalization in out-of-distribution settings.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a General-Purpose Compression Strategy for Deep Models: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a specialized technique for transferring softened output distributions into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across domains (vision, language, multimodal, and generative models). Empirical results across tasks show that KD can preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing model size and latency, and it can be combined with complementary strategies (pre-training, low-precision arithmetic, data synthesis, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints and privacy requirements. However, effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, attention maps), how teachers and students are aligned (layer mapping, input alignment), and whether real data are available (data-free or adversarially guided generation). This paper synthesizes evidence from recent work to argue that KD, when applied with these considerations, is a reliable foundation for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while preserving performance, enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, and domain-specific constraints. Across modalities and tasks, KD can be combined with architectural search, feature-level objectives, teacher optimization, and data-free methods to meet diverse production requirements. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a primary instrument in model-compression toolkits for modern deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teacher's performance. When combined with complementary strategies — such as careful layer mapping, pre-training of compact models, multi-teacher schedules, privacy-aware mechanisms, and synthetic-data techniques — distillation addresses the principal deployment barriers of modern deep networks: inference cost, data access constraints, and heterogeneous compute environments. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit that can be adapted to the needs of NLP and general deep learning applications to produce compact, robust, and privacy-conscious models.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and broadly applicable technique to compress large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Work across computer vision, speech, and natural language processing demonstrates that KD can enable deployment of resource-efficient models, improve generalization in constrained settings, and be combined with other compression methods (e.g., low-precision numerics). At the same time, the field has identified important limitations and nuanced behaviors — such as data simplification effects, teacher–student mismatches, and domain or task-specific failure modes — that guide how KD should be applied in practice. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, variants, empirical benefits, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation: Task-adaptive, Privacy-aware, and Feature-centric Compression for Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are now essential tools to deploy large deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. When applied thoughtfully—adapting to task requirements, leveraging feature-level signals, and accounting for data availability—KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher's performance while improving inference speed, memory footprint, and interpretability. However, naive distillation can fail under data heterogeneity, limited data, or strong teacher–student mismatches; addressing these requires task-aware layer selection, multi-teacher strategies, and alternatives to standard logit matching. I argue that the most effective KD pipelines combine task-adaptive compression, feature-directed supervision, and methods that preserve privacy and robustness to limited data.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become practical tools to reduce model size and computation while retaining much of the performance of large teachers. Across vision, speech, and natural language tasks, approaches include transferring soft logits, mimicking internal features or attention maps, layering/structural adaptations, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-preserving methods. Empirical results demonstrate that careful distillation can yield compact students that approach teacher accuracy and enable deployment in resource-constrained settings, but open challenges remain in robustness, task-specific distillation design, and distributed training dynamics.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Case for Richer Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a necessary and practical tool for compressing large models and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but its value depends critically on what is distilled and how. Soft-label matching transfers useful "dark knowledge" from ensembles, yet by itself often fails to capture internal structure, handle domain or data heterogeneity, or operate when original data are unavailable. Combining soft labels with internal- and feature-level guidance, architecture- and task-aware compression, and data- or privacy-aware generation strategies yields more robust, compact models that retain teacher performance across NLP and broader deep learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing deep models while preserving or even improving performance. Beyond the canonical soft-target distillation, variants that transfer internal representations, mimic features, adapt across modalities, and incorporate adversarial or online strategies make KD effective for many real-world constraints: limited compute, privacy/no-data settings, robustness requirements, ensemble compression, and large-scale distributed training. When applied thoughtfully—choosing the appropriate supervision signal (logits, features, attentions), architecture adapters (projectors), and training protocol (adversarial, online, or teacher-free)—distillation yields compact models that meet deployment constraints without sacrificing task performance.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expressive models to smaller, efficient models to enable practical deployment without excessive loss in performance. These methods include matching teacher soft outputs, feature-level alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and architecture-aware strategies for heterogeneous settings. Across domains—vision, speech, NLP, and recommender systems—distillation is used both to compress models for latency and memory constraints and to inject complementary knowledge (e.g., cross-task or cross-modal signals). Empirical work shows that careful design choices (e.g., mixing hard/soft targets, projector modules, or student-aware teacher training) and task-specific adaptations address common pitfalls such as information loss on rare tokens or domain shifts. Open directions include stronger theoretical understanding, robustness under imperfect teachers, and principled integration with quantization, federated settings, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, cheaper models (students) by using richer supervision than hard labels alone. The literature has developed multiple complementary strategies—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, architecturally guided replacement, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and teacher-training schemes—to address deployment constraints, domain shift, and limited or private data. Empirical work shows these approaches can close much of the performance gap to full-size models across classification, language understanding, and retrieval tasks; theoretical and empirical analyses explain why distillation often improves generalization beyond mere compression. Remaining challenges include input distribution mismatch, low-frequency token fidelity in sequence tasks, and robust distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Practices and Open Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from a high-capacity source (teacher) to a smaller target (student). Across vision, speech, and NLP, practitioners combine logit-based supervision, feature imitation, data augmentation, and architectural or precision changes to preserve performance while shrinking computation. Recent work emphasizes (1) the role of pre-training for compact models, (2) task- and modality-specific distillation recipes, (3) data-availability and privacy constraints that motivate data-free or augmentation-based approaches, and (4) designing teachers or training procedures that improve transfer. These trends point toward hybrid pipelines that integrate pre-training, augmentation, and teacher-student co-design to get robust, efficient models for real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer information from larger, more expensive models to smaller, cheaper models to reduce inference cost while retaining accuracy. Across computer vision, speech, recommender systems and natural language processing, KD variants have targeted soft-label transfer, relational or feature imitation, self-distillation, and teacher adaptation to improve student generalization. Practical work emphasizes complementary strategies — pretraining compact architectures, specialist teacher training, careful input augmentation, and training-time efficiency — to address optimization mismatch, domain shift, and computational overhead. Remaining challenges include imperfect matching between teacher and student distributions, choosing data and augmentation strategies that preserve useful teacher signals, and designing distillation procedures that scale to constrained hardware and domain-specific needs.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a core tool for shrinking large neural models into compact, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across domains — from language understanding and ranking to multimodal models and edge deployment — distillation enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and privacy that are otherwise difficult to achieve. However, consistent success requires more than naively matching teacher outputs: careful attention to student pre-training, layer alignment, task-aware selection of transferred signals, data augmentation, and deployment constraints (e.g., low-precision or federated scenarios) determines whether distillation yields practical gains. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated as a system-level design primitive rather than a single loss term, and it outlines methodological priorities to make distillation effective for NLP and deep learning practitioners.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large, high-performance models into smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from a teacher to a student. Recent work spans many complementary strategies — logit/soft-target matching, feature and layer-wise distillation, structural and channel-level transformations, data-free generation of proxy inputs, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and task-aware filtering — and addresses practical concerns such as cross-domain transfer, limited compute, and maintaining task performance in NLP settings. Progress includes specialized algorithms for pre-trained language model compression, algorithmic and architectural enhancements that reduce capacity gaps, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Together these developments offer a toolkit for deploying compact models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments while preserving most of the original model performance.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods have become central tools for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy and capabilities of large teachers. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of techniques—ranging from distilling logits, internal representations, and attention patterns to data-free and few-shot strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive search for student architectures. These approaches have been applied across vision, language, multimodal, and deployed/distributed settings, demonstrating substantial gains in inference speed and model size while exposing trade-offs in robustness, data requirements, and modality alignment. This survey summarizes the main algorithmic families, common engineering strategies, notable empirical outcomes, and key open challenges for applying distillation in practice.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or more informative models (teachers) into smaller or more efficient models (students). Research across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft-label matching, intermediate layer alignment, contrastive/representation losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, meta-learned teacher updates), and architecture-aware compression strategies (channel-wise attention, task-adaptive architecture search). Empirical and theoretical work highlights tradeoffs between bias and variance introduced by soft targets, the value of pre-training compact models before distillation, and the importance of data and augmentation choices for effective transfer. Emerging large-scale and privacy-aware deployments leverage online and federated distillation variants to reduce communication and improve reproducibility, while new approaches aim to make teachers more student-friendly or distill internal representations rather than only outputs. Key open challenges include matching representational structure across heterogeneous architectures, choosing what and when to distill, and scaling methods to very large datasets and distributed settings while preserving privacy and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have diversified from the original logits-based teacher→student paradigm into a broad set of methods that operate on features, modules, data, and training procedures. Contemporary work shows multiple complementary mechanisms for transferring knowledge—soft targets, feature- and attention-level mimicry, adversarial alignment, module replacement, and data- or communication-constrained distillation—each suited to different deployment constraints (privacy, compute, bandwidth) and model families (transformers, CNNs, GANs, GNNs). Advances emphasize (1) understanding why KD helps (stability, richer concept learning), (2) designing where to transfer knowledge (penultimate features, attention maps, projectors), and (3) tailoring the distillation process to practical settings (online multi-model training, federated environments, data-free scenarios, and teacher models optimized for students). Empirical results across vision, speech, language, generation, and retrieval indicate KD can yield compact models that retain most teacher performance when the distillation objective, the representation level, and the training dynamics are appropriately matched to the target constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression strategies have become central tools for shrinking large pretrained models into efficient deployable networks while preserving much of their performance. Methods range from transferring final-logit 'dark knowledge' to matching intermediate representations, attention maps, or feature distributions; from engineering compact student architectures to progressively replacing modules inside a single model. Applications span vision, speech, generative models, and NLP (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation), and extensions address scenarios with no access to original training data or heterogeneous, federated settings. Key trade-offs involve accuracy vs. size/latency, robustness and fairness, and the distributional assumptions needed for effective transfer. Important open problems include principled understanding of when and why distillation helps, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and reliably transferring robustness and inductive biases to small models.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or multi-modal models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural insights. Research has developed diverse KD variants—soft-label distillation, internal and layer-wise imitation, task-aware filtering, data-free distillation, and architecture-search guided compression—each addressing optimization, data availability, or deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs between matching teacher outputs and student generalization, the value of pre-training compact models, and the importance of choosing what and how knowledge is transferred to maximize downstream task performance while meeting resource limits.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transform large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster, and more deployable models while attempting to preserve accuracy and useful inductive biases. Approaches span classic teacher–student logit matching, representation and feature imitation, layer mapping strategies for large pretrained language models, data-free and zero-shot methods that avoid access to original training data, and privacy- or communication-aware frameworks for distributed settings. Empirical work demonstrates these methods can yield practical speedups, substantial parameter reductions, and competitive task performance across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks; theoretical and empirical studies also clarify when softened teacher targets or distilled datasets best help student capacity. Remaining challenges include balancing privacy and utility, reducing the cost of distillation when teachers are large, and extending guarantees and methods across modalities and domain shifts.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a General-Purpose Compression Strategy for Deep Models: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a specialized technique for transferring softened output distributions into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across domains (vision, language, multimodal, and generative models). Empirical results across tasks show that KD can preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing model size and latency, and it can be combined with complementary strategies (pre-training, low-precision arithmetic, data synthesis, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints and privacy requirements. However, effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, attention maps), how teachers and students are aligned (layer mapping, input alignment), and whether real data are available (data-free or adversarially guided generation). This paper synthesizes evidence from recent work to argue that KD, when applied with these considerations, is a reliable foundation for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a foundational technique for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. When applied thoughtfully — combining representational objectives, teacher-student co-design, task-aware compression, and appropriate data strategies — KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices while maintaining robustness and fairness. However, pitfalls arise from mismatches in inputs, teacher strength, data availability, and dataset biases; practical KD should therefore be integrated with complementary methods (e.g., architecture search, pruning, curriculum strategies, and data-generation) and with safeguards for ethical concerns.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large deep models into compact ones that are suitable for deployment. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and specialized tasks such as machine reading comprehension, KD enables students to inherit performance-critical behaviors from larger teachers while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in model size and compute. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., architecture search or structured pruning) and when tailored to task or domain specifics, distillation yields compressed models that approach teacher performance while meeting resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.
