papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models for deployment, while preserving performance and enabling new capabilities such as efficient federated learning, data-free compression, interpretability, and few-shot adaptation. Across architectures and tasks, KD variants—ranging from layer-to-layer alignment and progressive module replacement to meta-learned teachers and adversarial data synthesis—provide methods to trade computation, memory, and communication for small changes in accuracy. These methods make it possible to bring large pretrained models into production and edge settings, and to reconcile competing requirements such as privacy, heterogeneity, and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing modern deep models across modalities. When combined with architecture-aware transformations, feature-level supervision, multi-teacher signals, and careful handling of data constraints, KD enables compact students that retain most of a teacher's effectiveness while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, distillation artifacts and data limitations require methodic choices—e.g., feature mimicking, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, or generative replay—to avoid propagating teacher errors or overfitting in low-data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information from one or more teachers. Across vision and language applications, KD has been adapted to handle teacher-free scenarios, multi-teacher setups, intermediate representation alignment, data- and domain-shift, and task-specific constraints such as ranking or retrieval. Empirical work shows that distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while dramatically reducing model size and latency, but practical success depends on what is transferred (soft outputs, internal features, or relational/contrastive knowledge), the quality and heterogeneity of teacher data, and training design choices such as data augmentation and curriculum. The literature also highlights cases where naive distillation propagates teacher errors (e.g., low-frequency lexical mistakes) and where alternative strategies (label smoothing view, internal representation matching, dynamic teacher weighting, or curriculum selection of examples) yield measurable improvements. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, common pitfalls, and promising methods for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: The Strengths and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into deployable, efficient students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD can preserve task performance while drastically reducing size and compute, but its success depends on choices of what and how to transfer, availability and provenance of data, and training dynamics. Advances in feature-matching, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, data-free synthesis, and robustness-aware distillation expand KD's applicability but do not eliminate core challenges—optimization barriers, distribution heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and potential transfer of unwanted behaviors. A careful, task-aware combination of techniques is therefore required to realize reliable, compact models for production use.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying deep models in constrained environments. Work in this area spans simple teacher–student soft-label transfer to advanced feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial and data-free approaches, and automated search guided by distillation. Applications include compressing pre-trained language models, accelerating non-autoregressive translation, compressing generative models, and improving low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical studies highlight both practical recipes (mixing hard and soft labels, many-to-many layer mappings, feature mimicking) and conceptual explanations (connections to label smoothing and regularization), while open challenges remain in retaining rare-token behavior, mitigating bias transfer, and scaling distillation to privacy- or data-limited settings.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a single compression trick but a flexible set of techniques that can reduce model size, preserve or transfer task-relevant information, enable deployment in latency- and memory-constrained settings, support domain adaptation and privacy-preserving federated workflows, and be combined with structural compression. When applied thoughtfully — with task-aware selection of distilled signals, architecturally informed teacher-student design, and attention to data availability and optimization dynamics — KD yields large practical benefits for deep learning and NLP systems while avoiding common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: The Pragmatic Power and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a practical toolkit for shrinking models, transferring behavior across architectures and modalities, and enabling deployment under compute, memory, or privacy constraints. Beyond straightforward teacher-to-student compression, distillation techniques combine with data augmentation, synthetic-data generation, and regularization to address limited data, cross-domain gaps, and interpretability needs. However, outcomes depend on choices about teacher quality, training data availability, and objective design; careful method selection is required to realize reliable, production-ready gains.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: Practical, Theoretical, and Methodological Evidence for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and mature approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from richer teacher models to compact students. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, vision, graph learning, and retrieval—KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher's performance. Beyond pure compression, KD variants address practical deployment concerns: multi-teacher and confidence-aware schemes improve robustness to imperfect teachers; progressive and module-level replacement approaches enable deeper integrated compression; online/distillation-in-parallel techniques scale training and improve reproducibility; and targeted feature-distillation methods refine representational quality. Theory of wide networks provides guidance on when soft labels help and when mixing hard labels is beneficial. Together, empirical and theoretical work shows KD is a versatile, well-grounded toolbox for model compression and knowledge transfer in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models into smaller, more deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Contemporary work shows KD is not a single algorithm but a family of techniques that transfer knowledge via soft labels, intermediate feature supervision, layer-wise mappings, data augmentation, and even data-free synthesis. KD has been applied across modalities and tasks — from compressing large language and multimodal transformers to enabling lightweight generative models and resource-efficient inference on edge devices. Empirical and theoretical analyses have begun to explain when and why distillation works, how it transfers inductive biases, and which input-side interventions (e.g., mixup/CutMix variants) improve transfer. Practical challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and deciding what form of teacher knowledge (logits, features, relations, or structural priors) best serves a given student architecture.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Methods and Challenges in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across vision, generative modeling, and NLP, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, task-specific adaptations, multi-teacher schemes, and teacher-optimization strategies to improve student accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Work also focuses on constraints arising in distributed and privacy-preserving settings, on preserving rare or fine-grained information, and on adapting distillation to complex tasks such as detection, generation, and dense prediction. Practical systems combine architectural choices, training curricula, and distilled supervision to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured into a core tool for shrinking large neural models into compact, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across domains — from language understanding and ranking to multimodal models and edge deployment — distillation enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and privacy that are otherwise difficult to achieve. However, consistent success requires more than naively matching teacher outputs: careful attention to student pre-training, layer alignment, task-aware selection of transferred signals, data augmentation, and deployment constraints (e.g., low-precision or federated scenarios) determines whether distillation yields practical gains. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated as a system-level design primitive rather than a single loss term, and it outlines methodological priorities to make distillation effective for NLP and deep learning practitioners.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Beyond Dark Knowledge: A Practical Position on How and Why Knowledge Distillation Works for Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large models and adapting knowledge across architectures, domains, and devices. Its effectiveness derives from multiple mechanisms: soft-target regularization that shapes student generalization, representation-level transfer that preserves structure beyond logits, and methods that remove dependence on the teacher's training data. However, KD is not a single monolithic recipe — optimization dynamics, teacher-student mismatch, and interactions with other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing or fairness constraints) materially affect outcomes. I argue that practitioners should treat KD as a collection of complementary approaches (logit regularization, feature mimicking, contrastive alignment, data- or generator-based sample synthesis, and adaptive teacher selection) and choose combinations appropriate to their constraints (data availability, privacy, compute, heterogeneity). This perspective explains why simpler or even teacher-free approaches can match standard KD in many settings, and why representation- and adaptation-oriented variants expand KD’s applicability to domain adaptation, federated and graph models.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research spans algorithmic advances in teacher–student objectives, architecture-aware compression, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Practical work shows gains from combining KD with data augmentation, many-to-many layer mappings, and architecture search, while complementary efforts address data-free and privacy-preserving distillation. Remaining challenges include imperfect teachers, data heterogeneity, and adapting compression to task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods have become central tools for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy and capabilities of large teachers. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of techniques—ranging from distilling logits, internal representations, and attention patterns to data-free and few-shot strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive search for student architectures. These approaches have been applied across vision, language, multimodal, and deployed/distributed settings, demonstrating substantial gains in inference speed and model size while exposing trade-offs in robustness, data requirements, and modality alignment. This survey summarizes the main algorithmic families, common engineering strategies, notable empirical outcomes, and key open challenges for applying distillation in practice.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central family of techniques for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring information from larger (teacher) models or training dynamics into smaller (student) models. Across domains and modalities—vision, graph data, speech, and natural language—KD variants address different constraints: limited data or privacy, distributed training, domain shift, and task-specific requirements (e.g., ranking, generation, or sequence modeling). Mechanistically, KD leverages richer supervisory signals than hard labels (soft targets, intermediate features, relational structure, or training trajectories) to regularize students and often yields students that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory. Recent work has clarified connections between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing), introduced teacher-free and self-distillation approaches, explored the role of data augmentation and feature projectors, and adapted KD to federated, ensemble, and cross-task settings. Empirical results across tasks show KD can enable large compression/acceleration gains with modest performance loss and, in some settings, even improve generalization and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD techniques span soft-label transfer, intermediate representation matching, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, and adaptations for constrained or distributed settings. When combined with careful pretraining, representation-aware losses, selective sample strategies, and attention to privacy or robustness requirements, KD enables practical deployment of high-quality models on resource-limited devices and in federated environments.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Effective and Responsible Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Risks, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable deployment of large, high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from a cumbersome teacher to a compact student. KD delivers large gains in inference speed and memory while preserving much of the teacher's utility across NLP tasks (including question answering and sentence understanding) and other modalities. However, naive distillation can transfer undesirable properties such as bias, privacy leakage, or fragility to distribution shift and adversarial attacks. A combination of strategies—student-aware teacher design, multi-teacher curricula, selective sample distillation, data augmentation, adversarial and robust distillation, and privacy-aware ensembles—provides a pragmatic path to compress models while controlling fairness, robustness, and privacy trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing deep models while preserving or even improving performance. Beyond the canonical soft-target distillation, variants that transfer internal representations, mimic features, adapt across modalities, and incorporate adversarial or online strategies make KD effective for many real-world constraints: limited compute, privacy/no-data settings, robustness requirements, ensemble compression, and large-scale distributed training. When applied thoughtfully—choosing the appropriate supervision signal (logits, features, attentions), architecture adapters (projectors), and training protocol (adversarial, online, or teacher-free)—distillation yields compact models that meet deployment constraints without sacrificing task performance.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable smaller or faster models to retain much of the performance of larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or task-specific inductive biases. Work in this area spans supervised soft-target matching, intermediate-layer representation transfer, many-to-many layer alignment, data-free distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble-derived strategies, and online/distributed variants that exploit parallelism. Applications include compressing large pretrained language models for downstream NLP tasks, accelerating inference for computer vision and generative models, and producing interpretable or privacy-preserving compact models for healthcare and on-device deployment. Important trade-offs involve what form of knowledge is transferred (logits, activations, relations), access to training data, robustness to domain heterogeneity, and how to balance capacity, efficiency, and generalization in student models.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods have become central tools for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy and capabilities of large teachers. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of techniques—ranging from distilling logits, internal representations, and attention patterns to data-free and few-shot strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive search for student architectures. These approaches have been applied across vision, language, multimodal, and deployed/distributed settings, demonstrating substantial gains in inference speed and model size while exposing trade-offs in robustness, data requirements, and modality alignment. This survey summarizes the main algorithmic families, common engineering strategies, notable empirical outcomes, and key open challenges for applying distillation in practice.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, retrieval, visual recognition, graph-based prediction, and data-limited or privacy-constrained settings—distillation enables latency- and resource-constrained deployment. However, straightforward distillation is not a panacea: distribution shifts, heterogeneity of data and models, and absence of training data expose weaknesses that require complementary techniques (e.g., internal representation matching, layer mapping, task-aware selection, generative replay). Combining these advances yields compressed models that are both accurate and robust for real-world applications.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models for deployment, while preserving performance and enabling new capabilities such as efficient federated learning, data-free compression, interpretability, and few-shot adaptation. Across architectures and tasks, KD variants—ranging from layer-to-layer alignment and progressive module replacement to meta-learned teachers and adversarial data synthesis—provide methods to trade computation, memory, and communication for small changes in accuracy. These methods make it possible to bring large pretrained models into production and edge settings, and to reconcile competing requirements such as privacy, heterogeneity, and interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Strategy Path to Compressing Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large deep models while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and deployment settings, KD enables smaller models to inherit predictive behavior, internal structure, and cross-model insights from larger teachers. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary strategies — internal representation matching, curriculum scheduling, multi-teacher selection, data augmentation, meta-learned teachers, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols — yielding compact, efficient, and robust student models suitable for edge, federated, and low-precision deployments.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a single compression trick but a flexible set of techniques that can reduce model size, preserve or transfer task-relevant information, enable deployment in latency- and memory-constrained settings, support domain adaptation and privacy-preserving federated workflows, and be combined with structural compression. When applied thoughtfully — with task-aware selection of distilled signals, architecturally informed teacher-student design, and attention to data availability and optimization dynamics — KD yields large practical benefits for deep learning and NLP systems while avoiding common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation can be combined with architectural replacement, layer mapping, and task-adaptive search to produce compact models that meet latency and capacity constraints. However, the benefits of distillation depend strongly on teacher quality, data complexity, and which examples or representations are used for transfer; naive application can propagate teacher errors or harm low-frequency predictions. Careful design—using task-aware compression, selective or mixed supervision, and targeted remedies for dataset artifacts—enables distillation to deliver efficient, robust models for real-world NLP and vision systems.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or multi-modal models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural insights. Research has developed diverse KD variants—soft-label distillation, internal and layer-wise imitation, task-aware filtering, data-free distillation, and architecture-search guided compression—each addressing optimization, data availability, or deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs between matching teacher outputs and student generalization, the value of pre-training compact models, and the importance of choosing what and how knowledge is transferred to maximize downstream task performance while meeting resource limits.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Empirical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Approaches extend beyond matching soft logits to include intermediate-feature mimicry, attention-driven layer alignment, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive representation alignment, and task- or domain-aware search and adaptation. Empirical work shows KD is effective across modalities and tasks — from pre-trained language models and visual-linguistic systems to object detectors, recommender rankers, graph networks, and continual learning settings — but practical deployment requires addressing representation misalignment, task specificity, and catastrophic forgetting. This review synthesizes core strategies and key empirical findings to guide application and future research.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: The Strengths and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into deployable, efficient students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD can preserve task performance while drastically reducing size and compute, but its success depends on choices of what and how to transfer, availability and provenance of data, and training dynamics. Advances in feature-matching, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, data-free synthesis, and robustness-aware distillation expand KD's applicability but do not eliminate core challenges—optimization barriers, distribution heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and potential transfer of unwanted behaviors. A careful, task-aware combination of techniques is therefore required to realize reliable, compact models for production use.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Multi-purpose Strategy for Model Compression and Robust Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD supports domain adaptation, latency-aware architecture transformations, robustness transfer, and interpretable model surrogates. When combined with careful training protocols (e.g., multi-teacher schemes, domain adaptation, or targeted regularization), distillation enables deployment of high-performing models in resource- and latency-constrained or safety-critical settings across vision, speech, 3D perception, and natural language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, insights, and practical trends
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in latency-, memory-, and compute-constrained settings. Work across speech, NLP, vision, and graph domains demonstrates a spectrum of approaches: matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate features, progressively replacing modules, augmenting or synthesizing training data for better student generalization, and compressing ensembles into single models. Empirical results show substantial speed and size gains with modest accuracy loss when methods are carefully matched to task and architecture. Important themes include (1) the role of dark/soft labels vs. intermediate feature signals, (2) architectural or task-aware compression (including search), (3) techniques that increase the student’s exposure to informative training points (e.g., mixup or adversarial examples), and (4) distillation strategies tailored for ensembles or heterogeneous teacher–student pairs. Open challenges remain in principled sample selection, robust transfer of inductive biases, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and broadly applicable technique to compress large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Work across computer vision, speech, and natural language processing demonstrates that KD can enable deployment of resource-efficient models, improve generalization in constrained settings, and be combined with other compression methods (e.g., low-precision numerics). At the same time, the field has identified important limitations and nuanced behaviors — such as data simplification effects, teacher–student mismatches, and domain or task-specific failure modes — that guide how KD should be applied in practice. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, variants, empirical benefits, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.
