papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into deployable, efficient students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD can preserve task performance while drastically reducing size and compute, but its success depends on choices of what and how to transfer, availability and provenance of data, and training dynamics. Advances in feature-matching, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, data-free synthesis, and robustness-aware distillation expand KD's applicability but do not eliminate core challenges—optimization barriers, distribution heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and potential transfer of unwanted behaviors. A careful, task-aware combination of techniques is therefore required to realize reliable, compact models for production use.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Theory, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted approach to compress large deep models and transfer knowledge to smaller, faster, or more interpretable models. Across vision and language applications, KD encompasses teacher-student paradigms that use teacher soft targets, intermediate representations, or auxiliary objectives; extensions include multi-teacher setups, data-free distillation, meta-learned teachers, and device-aware distillation for heterogeneous deployments. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in parameters and inference cost; theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when and why distillation helps and how dataset complexity, teacher quality, and student capacity interact to determine outcomes. Practical strategies combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques to meet deployment constraints while retaining generalization.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD has proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling multimodal generation, compact evaluation metrics, and efficient inference. However, KD is not a black-box cure: its success depends on what is transferred (logits, features, intermediate layers), how teachers and students are paired or trained, and on optimization and regularization choices. I argue that KD should be viewed as a flexible toolkit—comprising feature-level mimicking, layer-aware projection, self- and teacher-free variants, and teacher-adaptation strategies—applied with careful attention to teacher-student interaction and training dynamics to achieve reliable compression in practice.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large neural networks for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Beyond simple model-size reduction, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving distributed training, data-free and zero-shot compression, and the transfer of adversarial robustness. Combining logit-based distillation with feature-level mimicking and carefully chosen regularization yields high-quality small models that remain competitive on downstream tasks in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Compressing and Deploying Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible technique that enables transferring predictive power from large models into smaller or more efficient ones. When combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, task-aware selection of distilled signals, quantization-aware training, and privacy-preserving or federated protocols, KD can make state-of-the-art models practically usable on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices. However, realizing these gains requires attention to what is distilled (outputs versus internal representations), how distilled signals are selected for the target task, and whether data-privacy or communication constraints demand synthetic or distributed distillation procedures.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a unifying strategy that addresses model size, inference latency, domain shifts, multimodal transfer, privacy, and training efficiency. By transferring supervisory signals, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger or more capable systems, KD enables compact student models to retain much of the performance of cumbersome teachers while meeting practical deployment constraints. When combined with task-aware architecture search, layer-mapping techniques, and online or domain-aware protocols, distillation offers a principled path to build small, fast, and adaptable models across diverse settings.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a versatile family of techniques that can preserve performance while enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but it must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. Effective KD requires attention to the teacher-student relationship (including training teachers that are "student-friendly"), to data availability (including data-free approaches), and to distributional mismatches (e.g., federated or heterogeneous-device scenarios). When such concerns are addressed—via task-adaptive compression, feature- or relation-aware transfer, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, or methods that expose raw data signals lost in naive distillation—KD can deliver near-teacher performance at far lower cost. However, KD has known failure modes (such as propagating teacher errors on low-frequency tokens or degrading under data heterogeneity) that demand targeted remedies. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an adaptable design pattern: choose techniques that match your downstream objective (accuracy, latency, privacy, heterogeneity) rather than applying a one-size-fits-all distillation loss.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary tools to shrink large deep models for deployment while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, speech and natural language processing, researchers have developed a range of approaches that operate at the level of logits (soft labels), intermediate representations, modules/layers, or training curricula, and have combined KD with complementary strategies such as architecture search, quantization, and generative replay. Empirical work shows that distilled students can often approach teacher performance while achieving large reductions in size and latency, but the effectiveness of different KD strategies depends strongly on task, data distribution, teacher strength, and practical constraints such as availability of original training data. Important challenges remain in transferring robustness, handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving rare-token behavior, and balancing bias–variance tradeoffs introduced by soft supervision.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or more informative models (teachers) into smaller or more efficient models (students). Research across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft-label matching, intermediate layer alignment, contrastive/representation losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, meta-learned teacher updates), and architecture-aware compression strategies (channel-wise attention, task-adaptive architecture search). Empirical and theoretical work highlights tradeoffs between bias and variance introduced by soft targets, the value of pre-training compact models before distillation, and the importance of data and augmentation choices for effective transfer. Emerging large-scale and privacy-aware deployments leverage online and federated distillation variants to reduce communication and improve reproducibility, while new approaches aim to make teachers more student-friendly or distill internal representations rather than only outputs. Key open challenges include matching representational structure across heterogeneous architectures, choosing what and when to distill, and scaling methods to very large datasets and distributed settings while preserving privacy and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation: Task-adaptive, Privacy-aware, and Feature-centric Compression for Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are now essential tools to deploy large deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. When applied thoughtfully—adapting to task requirements, leveraging feature-level signals, and accounting for data availability—KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher's performance while improving inference speed, memory footprint, and interpretability. However, naive distillation can fail under data heterogeneity, limited data, or strong teacher–student mismatches; addressing these requires task-aware layer selection, multi-teacher strategies, and alternatives to standard logit matching. I argue that the most effective KD pipelines combine task-adaptive compression, feature-directed supervision, and methods that preserve privacy and robustness to limited data.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compress large neural models into smaller, more deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Contemporary work shows KD is not a single algorithm but a family of techniques that transfer knowledge via soft labels, intermediate feature supervision, layer-wise mappings, data augmentation, and even data-free synthesis. KD has been applied across modalities and tasks — from compressing large language and multimodal transformers to enabling lightweight generative models and resource-efficient inference on edge devices. Empirical and theoretical analyses have begun to explain when and why distillation works, how it transfers inductive biases, and which input-side interventions (e.g., mixup/CutMix variants) improve transfer. Practical challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and deciding what form of teacher knowledge (logits, features, relations, or structural priors) best serves a given student architecture.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html."}, {'author': 'Pacheco', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary', 'abstract': 'Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.'}, {'author': 'Le', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living', 'abstract': 'Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\\times$ fewer parameters. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.'}, {'author': 'Parker', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a versatile family of techniques that can preserve performance while enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but it must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.'}, {'author': 'Parsons', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation', 'abstract': "Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. When applied thoughtfully—adapting to task requirements, leveraging feature-level signals, and accounting for data availability—KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher's performance while improving inference speed, memory footprint, and interpretability. KD has been applied across modalities and tasks — from compressing large language and multimodal transformers to enabling lightweight generative models and resource-efficient inference on edge devices. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.'}, {'author': 'Shaffer', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation', 'abstract': "Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Open Questions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses techniques that transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students). Across computer vision and natural language tasks, KD has been applied as logit-level supervision, feature mimicking, ensemble compression, self-distillation, domain-adaptive compression, and data-free/privacypreserving variants. Empirical work shows that distilled students can approach teacher performance while improving latency and footprint, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data complexity, and whether distillation occurs at the logits or feature level. Recent analyses link KD to label smoothing and show promising teacher-free or self-distillation approaches, while practical applications demonstrate domain-specific adaptation, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and techniques to mitigate degenerate behaviours in sequence generation. Remaining challenges include handling domain shift, preserving low-frequency lexical details, training without original data, and principled teacher selection.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring useful information from teacher models. Across vision, speech, reinforcement learning, and NLP, KD has been adapted into logit-level supervision, intermediate feature and layer-wise matching, data augmentation strategies, data-free setups, and training-time architectural replacement. Recent work has expanded KD to address practical constraints—privacy in federated settings, bias mitigation in language models, low-precision deployment, and multi-task transfer—while also proposing task-aware and capacity-aware methods to reduce redundant or harmful teacher signals. This synthesis summarizes the mechanisms, extensions, strengths, and limitations documented in contemporary studies and highlights promising directions for making distilled models both efficient and robust.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, researchers have developed logit-based distillation, feature- and attention-level mimicking, ensemble- and multi-teacher schemes, task-adaptive compression, and data- or teacher-free variants. These methods trade off compute, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness, and are often complementary to pruning and architecture search. Practical adoption favors combinations of pretraining, targeted distillation objectives, and adaptations to mismatches between teacher and student (e.g., inputs or architecture).

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation: Task-adaptive, Privacy-aware, and Feature-centric Compression for Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are now essential tools to deploy large deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. When applied thoughtfully—adapting to task requirements, leveraging feature-level signals, and accounting for data availability—KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher's performance while improving inference speed, memory footprint, and interpretability. However, naive distillation can fail under data heterogeneity, limited data, or strong teacher–student mismatches; addressing these requires task-aware layer selection, multi-teacher strategies, and alternatives to standard logit matching. I argue that the most effective KD pipelines combine task-adaptive compression, feature-directed supervision, and methods that preserve privacy and robustness to limited data.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Complementary Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, flexible route to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher’s capability. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, variants of KD — including multi-teacher schemes, internal-representation matching, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, and data-free approaches — have shown that distilled students can approach or even match teacher performance. KD is also complementary to pruning and quantization, enabling stacked compression pipelines that meet strict hardware constraints. I argue KD should be a first-line technique for model compression in deep learning and NLP, applied in combination with other resource-aware methods and chosen variants adapted to data availability and task structure.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance characteristics from larger models. Research has introduced multiple KD paradigms—teacher-student soft-label transfer, self-distillation, feature/internal-representation matching, multi-teacher strategies, and data-augmentation–aware distillation—each addressing different practical constraints such as domain shift, resource limits, or heterogeneous architectures. Applications span speech, machine translation evaluation, ASR, and domain-specific pretrained models; empirical work shows substantial reductions in model size and latency can be achieved with modest accuracy loss, or sometimes even gains, when distillation is combined with architectural adaptations and training-time strategies. Remaining challenges include transferring internal representations across heterogeneous architectures, choosing or designing teachers that are most useful for particular students, and preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals during aggressive compression.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) into smaller, cheaper models (students) by using richer supervision than hard labels alone. The literature has developed multiple complementary strategies—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, architecturally guided replacement, multi-teacher schedules, data- and privacy-aware variants, and teacher-training schemes—to address deployment constraints, domain shift, and limited or private data. Empirical work shows these approaches can close much of the performance gap to full-size models across classification, language understanding, and retrieval tasks; theoretical and empirical analyses explain why distillation often improves generalization beyond mere compression. Remaining challenges include input distribution mismatch, low-frequency token fidelity in sequence tasks, and robust distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a pragmatic and flexible approach to compressing large neural models so they can be deployed under memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. KD enables substantial reductions in size and compute while retaining much of a teacher model's performance, and it adapts well to modalities from vision to speech and to task-specific constraints in NLP. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, mismatches between teacher and student, and the potential for poorer outcomes when distilling inappropriate teacher signals require careful method selection and evaluation. Best practice therefore combines tailored distillation architectures, curriculum or multi-teacher strategies, privacy-aware mechanisms where needed, and awareness of when label-smoothing or teacher-free alternatives are preferable.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compressing and Deploying Large NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible approach to compress large deep models so they can be deployed under latency, storage, and privacy constraints. By transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations from a high-capacity teacher to a smaller student, KD enables large pre-trained NLP models to be adapted, accelerated, and sometimes even improved for downstream tasks and specific domains. Effective KD requires careful design choices—how to match intermediate layers, whether to rely on data or synthesize surrogates, how to combine multiple teachers, and how to account for fairness and domain shift. When combined with complementary compression techniques, KD becomes a core component of production-ready model compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary tools to shrink large deep models for deployment while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, speech and natural language processing, researchers have developed a range of approaches that operate at the level of logits (soft labels), intermediate representations, modules/layers, or training curricula, and have combined KD with complementary strategies such as architecture search, quantization, and generative replay. Empirical work shows that distilled students can often approach teacher performance while achieving large reductions in size and latency, but the effectiveness of different KD strategies depends strongly on task, data distribution, teacher strength, and practical constraints such as availability of original training data. Important challenges remain in transferring robustness, handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving rare-token behavior, and balancing bias–variance tradeoffs introduced by soft supervision.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: The Role and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. KD is applicable across modalities and tasks, from machine translation and reading comprehension to distributed training and privacy-sensitive deployment. Success depends on aligning teacher and student representations, selecting appropriate knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention, contrastive signals), and matching methods to constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy requirements. Theoretical analyses and practical advances both show that careful design choices — including attention-based matching, layer projection, task-aware filtering, online collaboration, multi-teacher weighting, and privacy-aware perturbation — materially affect outcomes and trade-offs between fidelity, efficiency, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Tradeoffs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers behaviors of larger or differently structured models into smaller or alternative models by training students to match teacher outputs, intermediate representations, or other derived supervision signals. Empirically, distillation improves deployment efficiency, can transfer inductive biases and robustness properties, and enables compression across domains including classification, generation, speech, and transformers. Success depends on choices such as what to transfer (logits, features, attention, or synthetic labels), how to combine hard and soft targets, privacy/robustness constraints, and whether teachers are perfect. Contemporary work links distillation to regularization and label smoothing, proposes layer-level and adversarial methods, and demonstrates broad applicability while highlighting limitations tied to teacher quality, data distribution, and adversarial vulnerability.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying deep models under resource constraints. Methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include intermediate-layer supervision, feature mimicking, projector-based transforms, teacher-student co-training, and data- or domain-aware schemes. Distillation has been applied across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs) and in settings with limited or no access to original training data. Practical advances address transfer across architectures, task-adaptive compression, and efficient architecture search, while open problems remain around distribution shift, heterogeneity of data or detectors, and preserving rare or low-frequency information.
