papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Practical Case for Richer Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a necessary and practical tool for compressing large models and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings, but its value depends critically on what is distilled and how. Soft-label matching transfers useful "dark knowledge" from ensembles, yet by itself often fails to capture internal structure, handle domain or data heterogeneity, or operate when original data are unavailable. Combining soft labels with internal- and feature-level guidance, architecture- and task-aware compression, and data- or privacy-aware generation strategies yields more robust, compact models that retain teacher performance across NLP and broader deep learning tasks.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing modern deep models across modalities. When combined with architecture-aware transformations, feature-level supervision, multi-teacher signals, and careful handling of data constraints, KD enables compact students that retain most of a teacher's effectiveness while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, distillation artifacts and data limitations require methodic choices—e.g., feature mimicking, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, or generative replay—to avoid propagating teacher errors or overfitting in low-data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or complex models into smaller, faster, or more constrained students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from a teacher. Over the past decade this has produced a diverse set of recipes — from logits/soft-label supervision to feature and layer-wise matching, progressive module replacement, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, and distributed/online variants — that together address deployment, privacy, robustness, and resource heterogeneity. Empirical work demonstrates that distilled students can approach teacher performance in NLP and vision tasks while enabling faster inference, lower memory use, or operation on weak devices; theoretical and empirical analyses illuminate when soft labels help, when hard labels or sample selection are needed, and how augmentation or task-aware selection of teacher knowledge improves transfer. Remaining challenges include principled understanding of which teacher signals are most useful for a given target task and resource constraint, robust and private distillation without original data, and scalable distillation in large distributed training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones that are deployable in resource-constrained settings. A rich set of distillation strategies has been developed: matching teacher output distributions, transferring intermediate representations, adversarial or data-free synthesis of training examples, multi-teacher aggregation, and contrastive or projector-based representation alignment. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many tasks (including NLP and graph learning), but practical success depends strongly on optimization details, the availability and alignment of data, and careful design of the distillation objective. Privacy-preserving variants and methods tailored to domain-specific architectures (e.g., GNNs, transformers) extend KD’s applicability, while also introducing trade-offs between utility, robustness, and guarantees. This synthesis summarizes key methods, empirical findings, and known limitations to guide research and practice in KD for deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance characteristics from larger models. Research has introduced multiple KD paradigms—teacher-student soft-label transfer, self-distillation, feature/internal-representation matching, multi-teacher strategies, and data-augmentation–aware distillation—each addressing different practical constraints such as domain shift, resource limits, or heterogeneous architectures. Applications span speech, machine translation evaluation, ASR, and domain-specific pretrained models; empirical work shows substantial reductions in model size and latency can be achieved with modest accuracy loss, or sometimes even gains, when distillation is combined with architectural adaptations and training-time strategies. Remaining challenges include transferring internal representations across heterogeneous architectures, choosing or designing teachers that are most useful for particular students, and preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals during aggressive compression.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Empirical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a diverse set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Approaches extend beyond matching soft logits to include intermediate-feature mimicry, attention-driven layer alignment, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive representation alignment, and task- or domain-aware search and adaptation. Empirical work shows KD is effective across modalities and tasks — from pre-trained language models and visual-linguistic systems to object detectors, recommender rankers, graph networks, and continual learning settings — but practical deployment requires addressing representation misalignment, task specificity, and catastrophic forgetting. This review synthesizes core strategies and key empirical findings to guide application and future research.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Work across vision and language shows a set of recurring strategies: transfer using softened outputs (soft targets), imitation of intermediate/internal representations, layer mapping between teacher and student, task-adaptive architecture search, self-distillation, and data-free distillation when original training data are unavailable. Empirical results indicate that properly designed distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while offering large gains in inference speed and memory; however, success depends on which knowledge is transferred (outputs vs. internal features), how layers are aligned, and whether task specificity and data availability are addressed. The field currently balances practical engineering (architecture and search) with algorithmic refinements (losses and training regimes), and open challenges include robust data-free methods, principled many-to-many layer matching, and teacher designs that are optimized to be “student-friendly.”

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide effective ways to reduce the computational and memory costs of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Approaches span soft-target (logit) distillation, feature- and layer-level matching, data-augmentation and data-free techniques, and multi-teacher or teacher-optimization strategies. Recent work emphasizes task-aware alignment between teacher and student representations, augmentation schemes that improve teacher-student consistency, and training teachers that are explicitly optimized to help downstream students, enabling more reliable deployment in low-resource and privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, researchers have developed logit-based distillation, feature- and attention-level mimicking, ensemble- and multi-teacher schemes, task-adaptive compression, and data- or teacher-free variants. These methods trade off compute, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness, and are often complementary to pruning and architecture search. Practical adoption favors combinations of pretraining, targeted distillation objectives, and adaptations to mismatches between teacher and student (e.g., inputs or architecture).

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic training trick into a unifying framework for producing compact, efficient models across vision, speech, and language tasks. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus from larger teachers to smaller students, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while largely preserving accuracy. Beyond plain size reduction, KD adapts to constraints that arise in real deployments — limited data or privacy-sensitive settings, heterogeneous architectures, and modality gaps — through techniques such as feature-level alignment, selective sampling, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data-free synthesis. As a practical bridge between research-scale architectures and deployable systems, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and serves both as an efficiency accelerator and as a lever for robustness and domain generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods have become central tools for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy and capabilities of large teachers. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of techniques—ranging from distilling logits, internal representations, and attention patterns to data-free and few-shot strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and task-adaptive search for student architectures. These approaches have been applied across vision, language, multimodal, and deployed/distributed settings, demonstrating substantial gains in inference speed and model size while exposing trade-offs in robustness, data requirements, and modality alignment. This survey summarizes the main algorithmic families, common engineering strategies, notable empirical outcomes, and key open challenges for applying distillation in practice.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool: Compression, Regularization, and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression heuristic into a versatile training paradigm that enables model size reduction, improved generalization, domain adaptation, and task consolidation. Its practical success depends on both the sources of teacher supervision (final logits, intermediate representations, or multiple teachers) and how distillation is applied (sample selection, layer matching, or label design). While KD frequently yields compact, high-performing models, its benefits arise from a mixture of transferred dark knowledge and regularizing effects of soft targets; careful design choices are required to realize those benefits across settings such as language model compression, multi-task training, and privacy-constrained or heterogeneous environments.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Insights in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer useful information from larger, more expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable models. Research spans theoretical analyses of what is transferred, architectural and loss-design strategies to improve feature and output matching, specialized teacher–student training regimes (including multi-teacher and student-aware teacher training), online and federated distillation for large-scale or privacy-sensitive settings, and structural compression strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing memory and compute. Applications include image models, generative models, question-answering systems and multi-task natural language understanding, with methods tailored to domain constraints such as heterogeneous device capabilities and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression approaches seek to transfer useful information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, deployable student models while preserving performance. Research has expanded beyond matching final logits to include feature- and layer-level supervision, adaptive layer alignments, many-to-many mappings, task-aware filtering, teacher-free alternatives, data- and communication-constrained settings, and careful use of input-side techniques such as data augmentation. Empirical work shows these strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy across vision and language tasks, and practical pipelines combine pre-training of compact architectures with targeted distillation to improve downstream performance and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large deep models into compact ones that are suitable for deployment. Across NLP, speech, vision-language, and specialized tasks such as machine reading comprehension, KD enables students to inherit performance-critical behaviors from larger teachers while enabling orders-of-magnitude reductions in model size and compute. When combined with complementary techniques (e.g., architecture search or structured pruning) and when tailored to task or domain specifics, distillation yields compressed models that approach teacher performance while meeting resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Principled Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical technique for compressing large neural models into deployable, efficient students while preserving much of teacher performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, multi-task, and low-precision settings, distillation can recover large-model accuracy in smaller footprints when combined with careful design choices that address capacity mismatch, task relevance, and the nature of the transferred knowledge. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on distillation schedule, selection of what to transfer (logits, features, or task-aware subsets), and occasionally on teacher improvement or specialization. Understanding these interactions is key to robust compression for production NLP and deep-learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller ones to reduce inference cost, improve deployability, or impart desirable properties (robustness, fairness, interpretability). Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, ensemble consensus, attention maps) and in what data is available (original training data, synthetic data, or no data). Practical systems combine KD with architecture-level compression (pruning, structured sparsity) and with training-time strategies (online or continual distillation, curriculum schedules) to trade off efficiency and accuracy. While KD yields strong empirical results across NLP, speech, vision, and generative models, open challenges remain in data-free settings, cross-domain generalization, preserving fairness and interpretability, and designing distillation objectives that best capture the teacher’s knowledge for a given task.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teacher's performance. When combined with complementary strategies — such as careful layer mapping, pre-training of compact models, multi-teacher schedules, privacy-aware mechanisms, and synthetic-data techniques — distillation addresses the principal deployment barriers of modern deep networks: inference cost, data access constraints, and heterogeneous compute environments. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit that can be adapted to the needs of NLP and general deep learning applications to produce compact, robust, and privacy-conscious models.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable smaller, faster models to inherit performance characteristics from larger models. Research has introduced multiple KD paradigms—teacher-student soft-label transfer, self-distillation, feature/internal-representation matching, multi-teacher strategies, and data-augmentation–aware distillation—each addressing different practical constraints such as domain shift, resource limits, or heterogeneous architectures. Applications span speech, machine translation evaluation, ASR, and domain-specific pretrained models; empirical work shows substantial reductions in model size and latency can be achieved with modest accuracy loss, or sometimes even gains, when distillation is combined with architectural adaptations and training-time strategies. Remaining challenges include transferring internal representations across heterogeneous architectures, choosing or designing teachers that are most useful for particular students, and preserving low-frequency or domain-specific signals during aggressive compression.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Motivations, and Open Questions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a set of techniques that transfer information from larger or more complex models (teachers) to smaller or more efficient models (students). These practices are used both to reduce inference cost and to adapt large models to constrained or specialized settings (privacy-preserving deployment, edge devices, or faster generation). Across applications—classification, sequence modeling, graph learning, speech, and machine translation—research has explored what to transfer (logits, features, representations), how to transfer it (soft labels, feature projectors, adversarial objectives, data augmentation), and when transfer can fail or require modification (noisy labels, distributional shifts, imperfect teachers). Empirical and theoretical work shows benefits but also identifies trade-offs (regularization vs. fidelity, robustness transfer limits, and data requirements), motivating hybrid approaches that combine pre-training, careful sample selection, and augmentation.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer information from larger, more expensive models to smaller, cheaper models to reduce inference cost while retaining accuracy. Across computer vision, speech, recommender systems and natural language processing, KD variants have targeted soft-label transfer, relational or feature imitation, self-distillation, and teacher adaptation to improve student generalization. Practical work emphasizes complementary strategies — pretraining compact architectures, specialist teacher training, careful input augmentation, and training-time efficiency — to address optimization mismatch, domain shift, and computational overhead. Remaining challenges include imperfect matching between teacher and student distributions, choosing data and augmentation strategies that preserve useful teacher signals, and designing distillation procedures that scale to constrained hardware and domain-specific needs.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Path to Compressing and Deploying Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible technique that enables transferring predictive power from large models into smaller or more efficient ones. When combined with complementary strategies such as pre-training of compact architectures, task-aware selection of distilled signals, quantization-aware training, and privacy-preserving or federated protocols, KD can make state-of-the-art models practically usable on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices. However, realizing these gains requires attention to what is distilled (outputs versus internal representations), how distilled signals are selected for the target task, and whether data-privacy or communication constraints demand synthetic or distributed distillation procedures.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches to Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques produce smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teachers to compact students. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed diverse strategies—teacher–student logits matching, layer-wise representation matching, adversarial sample generation, progressive module replacement, many-to-many layer mapping, and task-aware filtering—to address capacity gaps, data access limits, privacy constraints, and robustness needs. Practical deployments additionally combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, and federated protocols to meet hardware and communication budgets. Empirical work shows that careful design of distillation objectives and inputs can preserve most of the teacher’s accuracy and even transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, while specialized schemes enable distillation without original training data or across continual/heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and pragmatic framework for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or more private models across modalities and tasks. When applied thoughtfully — by matching outputs, intermediate representations, training dynamics, or ensembles — KD can preserve or even improve task performance while enabling low-latency inference, reduced memory/compute, and new deployment modes (e.g., federated, data-free, or low-precision). However, distillation is not automatic: design choices about what to transfer, when to transfer, and how to align teacher and student matter for robustness, domain shifts, and rare-token behavior. I argue that best practice combines representation-aware objectives, selective or collaborative teaching strategies, and deployment-aware constraints (privacy, communication, numeric precision) to realize the full benefits of distillation in NLP and other deep learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD has proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling multimodal generation, compact evaluation metrics, and efficient inference. However, KD is not a black-box cure: its success depends on what is transferred (logits, features, intermediate layers), how teachers and students are paired or trained, and on optimization and regularization choices. I argue that KD should be viewed as a flexible toolkit—comprising feature-level mimicking, layer-aware projection, self- and teacher-free variants, and teacher-adaptation strategies—applied with careful attention to teacher-student interaction and training dynamics to achieve reliable compression in practice.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a single-teacher trick into a versatile family of methods that enable deployable, compact models across vision and language tasks. Empirical work across domains shows that distillation benefits from adopting strategies that reflect (1) where the student starts (pre-training), (2) what signals it receives (single, multi- or ensemble teachers; feature- and layer-level targets), and (3) the constraints of the deployment context (limited or no access to real data, heterogenous devices, or federated settings). Combining these insights yields practical recipes that reliably close the gap between large models and resource-constrained students while preserving robustness and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, cheaper students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, methods range from classic teacher-student logits supervision to data-free and online schemes, meta-learned teachers, and representation-level transfers. Empirical work shows KD often yields substantial efficiency gains but its effectiveness depends on dataset complexity, model capacity, data availability, and optimization choices; important failure modes and practical remediation strategies have been identified.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a unifying, practical framework to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while addressing concerns of computation, privacy, robustness, and limited task data. KD techniques span from logits- and feature-based matching to progressive module replacement, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free (zero-shot) synthesis, and federated output-sharing, and when combined with careful data augmentation and generative replay they yield compact models that retain much of the teacher utility in real-world settings.

Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.'}, {'author': 'Adams', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation', 'abstract': 'The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers.
